justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the asset across all three horizons, with the 1-day estimate of 173.5 anchored closely to what was likely the prevailing market price at the time of the forecast. The slight upward drift from 1-day to 1-week (175.0) and 1-month (178.0) captures a gentle positive trend assumption, consistent with either a gradual recovery pattern or modest fundamental tailwinds I would have been observing. The incremental increases are deliberately small because I was not assuming any strong directional catalyst, but rather a mild continuation of existing momentum or mean-reversion toward a perceived fair value slightly above the then-current price.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a manner consistent with standard uncertainty compounding over time. At 1-day, the 90% CI spans roughly 17 points (165–182), reflecting normal intraday and overnight volatility. By 1-week, the range expands to 34 points, and by 1-month it reaches 62 points, accounting for the accumulation of macroeconomic releases, earnings surprises, and sentiment shifts that can meaningfully redirect prices over longer windows. The asymmetry in the intervals — roughly symmetric around the point estimate — suggests I was not strongly tilting toward a skewed distribution in either direction at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include unexpected macroeconomic shocks such as a surprise central bank policy shift, an inflation print far outside consensus, or a deterioration in credit conditions that triggers broad risk-off selling. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a geopolitical resolution reducing uncertainty, or a sudden surge in institutional buying could push prices well above 210 on a 1-month basis. Liquidity events or flash crashes, though low probability, represent tail risks that could temporarily breach even wide intervals.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, while appearing wide in absolute terms, may still understate true tail risk. Markets occasionally experience regime changes — such as the onset of a financial crisis or a sudden policy pivot — that render historical volatility patterns poor guides to future uncertainty. If such a regime shift occurred within the forecast window, outcomes far outside my stated ranges would be entirely plausible, and this structural limitation is inherent to any probabilistic forecast built on recent historical data.
